unit_label: BFM Module C unit 4 (courseware unit 22): funding and regulatory aspects

facts.statement: Money supply and reserve assets (courseware): the central bank is the note issuing authority, so currency in circulation is directly controlled by it; but currency is a small part of total money. Cash deposited in banks is lent again, creating new deposits (the money multiplier effect: money created through relending); near cash instruments such as cheques and credit cards also add to the money supply. Money in circulation is measured by broad money (M3), which includes currency in circulation, demand and time deposits with banks and post office savings deposits. The money multiplier is M3 divided by reserve money. Monetary policy aims at controlling inflation and ensuring stability of financial markets (including foreign exchange markets); to do so the central bank must exercise control over M3. Reserve money is impounded by means of the cash reserve ratio (CRR), intended to reduce the money multiplier. Reserve assets are the cash deposited by scheduled commercial banks with the central bank for the CRR and funds invested in government and other approved securities for the SLR; they also serve as a cushion to banks.

CRR and SLR: definition and legal basis (courseware): CRR, under the central bank Act (section 42) and the Banking Regulation Act (section 18), is the amount of funds that all scheduled commercial banks must maintain with the central bank, expressed as a percentage of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL); it is a mandatory deposit with the central bank. SLR, under section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, is the prescribed percentage of NDTL a bank must hold in prescribed liquid assets (cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities, mostly government securities) at the close of business every day. The statutory minimum and maximum limits were removed by amendments in 2006 and 2007, so the central bank can stipulate the ratio at its discretion. The courseware notes that the prescriptions are intended to cushion the bank; the central bank would act as lender of last resort in an extreme case of distress. The CRR and SLR together are quantitative tools of monetary policy: an increase impounds cash resources (absorbing liquidity); a decrease releases funds (infusing liquidity). The figures stated in the courseware (4.50 per cent and 18 per cent) are as at 2022 and are not taught.

Why liquidity matters and treasury duty (courseware): liquidity is surplus funds with banks, an indicator of money supply not absorbed by the real economy; excess liquidity may lead to inflation, while a shortage may raise interest rates and depreciate the exchange rate. The central bank calibrates interest rates and adopts a policy stance consistent with the projected growth rate of the economy; with the removal of most exchange controls it no longer targets a specific exchange rate but monitors and irons out volatility. Treasury primary responsibility is to meet the CRR and SLR requirements fully; the back office must submit the relevant information to the central bank in the fortnightly return within the time schedule. Default or shortfall attracts serious penalties and damages the bank reputation and viability.

Demand and time liabilities (courseware): demand liabilities are those payable on demand: current deposits, the demand portion of savings deposits, margins against letters of credit and guarantees, balances in overdue fixed deposits, cash certificates and cumulative or recurring deposits, outstanding telegraphic transfers, mail transfers and demand drafts, unclaimed deposits, credit balances in cash credit accounts, and deposits held as security for advances payable on demand. Money at call and short notice from outside the banking system is shown against liability to others. Time liabilities are payable otherwise than on demand: fixed deposits, cash certificates, cumulative and recurring deposits, the time portion of savings deposits, staff security deposits, margins held against letters of credit not payable on demand, deposits held as securities for advances not payable on demand and gold deposits. Specified liabilities are exempt from or excluded from the CRR base (for example liabilities to the banking system in India, credit balances in Asian Currency Unit accounts, liabilities of offshore banking units, paid-up capital, reserves, retained profits and refinance from the central bank and apex institutions); the full lists and later changes are not taught.

Computation, maintenance and penalty (courseware): the CRR is computed on the NDTL as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight (a lag of one fortnight, so banks have time to collect data from branches). Banks maintain cash balances on average over the fortnight, subject to daily balances not falling below a stated share (90 per cent in the courseware) of the required amount, giving flexibility to scheduled commercial banks; the flexibility does not apply to urban co-operative banks. Scheduled commercial banks maintain CRR as balances with the central bank only (branch cash is not eligible), while for urban co-operative banks branch cash is also eligible. No interest is paid on CRR balances, so the CRR effectively increases the cost of deposits to the banking sector. The SLR is computed on the same NDTL base and lag; the exemptions from CRR liabilities do not apply to the SLR base in the same way. SLR assets: cash balances (excluding CRR balances), gold valued at a price not exceeding the current market price and approved securities valued as per the central bank norms (almost entirely government securities including treasury bills). Penalty: a shortfall in CRR attracts penal interest at a stated rate above the Bank Rate on the shortfall amount, rising if it continues; SLR shortfall attracts penal interest under the Banking Regulation Act. Rates are not taught. A change in the reserve ratios changes money supply: a 0.5 per cent cut in CRR releases a large amount of cash (the courseware estimates Rs 80,000-85,000 crore) which flows into bank credit or investment.

Worked CRR and SLR illustration (courseware): for a fortnight, NDTL as at the relevant last Friday multiplied by the required ratios gives the CRR and SLR to be maintained; the courseware example shows NDTL Rs 1,20,000 crore, CRR at 4.5 per cent = Rs 5,400 crore and SLR at 18 per cent = Rs 21,600 crore for the fortnight, and the next fortnight uses the new NDTL of Rs 1,30,000 crore. Every scheduled bank, small finance bank and payment bank must keep not less than a stated share of the required CRR on all days during the reporting fortnight, so that the average of daily CRR balances is not less than the prescribed CRR.

Liquidity Adjustment Facility (courseware): the LAF is the principal operating instrument of monetary policy; while CRR and SLR change the stance more permanently, the LAF is used to manage day-to-day liquidity. Under repo the central bank lends funds to banks against government securities (a purchase with an agreement to sell back); under reverse repo it absorbs surplus funds from banks (a sale with an agreement to buy back). The securities are held in the SGL account so no physical transfer takes place. The central bank, as lender of last resort, provides liquidity through repo auctions or fixed rate repo; the interest is the difference between sale and repurchase price. Auctions are held daily for overnight funds, possibly twice or thrice a day since banks need liquidity for payment obligations through the RTGS. Minimum bid amount applies. The central bank can change the term of repo and accept or reject bids. Instruments under the LAF framework for short-term liquidity: the 14-day variable rate repo or reverse repo auction (main operation, on the reporting Friday), variable rate term repo or reverse repo for fine-tuning (overnight to 13 days), the fixed rate reverse repo, the marginal standing facility (MSF), FX swap auctions and the standing deposit facility (SDF, operational from April 2022, replacing the fixed rate reverse repo as the floor). Instruments for durable liquidity: long term variable rate repo and reverse repo (tenor beyond 14 days), FX swap and open market operations. Amounts, rates and timings are as at 2022 and not taught.

Policy rate corridor (courseware): the objective of monetary policy is to narrow the policy rate corridor to align the weighted average call rate (WACR) with the repo rate. The SDF rate is the floor (the minimum rate of interest on excess funds) and the MSF rate is the ceiling (the maximum rate at which banks can borrow overnight when other funds are not available), with the repo rate in the middle. By restricting overnight rates within the corridor the central bank reduces fluctuations in short-term rates and, by moving either side of the corridor, can increase or decrease interest rates without directly regulating them; repo is used as a market-based instrument or benchmark rate to carry out policy objectives. The central bank has issued master directions for call, notice and term money operations for banks and primary dealers within limits set by their boards.

Payment and settlement systems (courseware): payments are inter-bank payments and payments on behalf of customers; settlement is payment or receipt in exchange of securities or foreign exchange. Conventionally inter-bank payments were net-settled through the clearing house, with delays of one to three days, counterparty risk and high cost in paper-based cheque clearing. Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS): a paperless clearing system where settlement is on a gross basis (transaction by transaction) in real time rather than a day-end net settlement; inter-bank payments and large customer remittances (above a minimum amount) are settled instantly; banks need adequate funds with the central bank throughout the day, and the central bank provides intra-day liquidity through automatic repo against securities lodged. Messaging: INFINET (secure communication backbone) and SFMS, a structured financial messaging system similar to SWIFT, the international system. Negotiated Dealing System (NDS): an electronic platform for dealing in government securities and money market instruments with automatic reporting and settlement, auctions on an electronic platform and quote-driven trading; NDS-OM is an anonymous order matching system where the identity of the counterparty is not disclosed and orders are matched on price and time priority; trades flow with straight-through processing to the clearing corporation (CCIL) for settlement. All dealings in government securities are on NDS; deals done outside it must be reported. CCIL is the central counterparty for clearing of government securities, repo and TREPS. FX Clear is a forex dealing system for USD/INR and cross currencies, with the clearing corporation as intermediary settling inter-bank deals on a net basis. Depositories (NSDL and CDSL) provide delivery versus payment for secondary market deals in equity and debt, eliminating settlement risk since funds and securities move simultaneously. NEFT: electronic funds transfer with same-day settlement, sorted and cleared by a national clearing cell; core banking solutions let funds move instantly between branches. The central bank has a board for regulation and supervision of payment and settlement systems.

payload.title: Money supply, the money multiplier and reserve assets
payload.core_explanation_md:
The central bank is the **note issuing authority**, so it directly controls **currency in circulation**, but currency is only a **small part** of total money.

- Cash deposited in banks is **lent again**, creating **new deposits**: the **money multiplier effect**. **Cheques and credit cards** (near cash) add to money supply.
- **Broad money (M3)** = **currency in circulation + demand and time deposits with banks + post office savings deposits**.
- **Money multiplier = M3 / reserve money.**
- Monetary policy aims to **control inflation** and keep **financial markets (including forex) stable**, so the central bank must **control M3**.
- **Reserve money** is impounded through the **CRR**, which **lowers the multiplier**.

**Reserve assets** are the **cash kept with the central bank (CRR)** and funds invested in **government and other approved securities (SLR)**. They also **cushion** the bank.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A higher multiplier means each rupee of reserve money supports more deposits.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the money multiplier defined?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Broad money (M3) divided by reserve money.

payload.title: CRR and SLR: meaning, basis and monetary role
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **CRR** | **SLR** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | Share of **NDTL** kept **as cash balance with the central bank** | Share of **NDTL** held in **liquid assets** |
| **Assets** | **Cash with the central bank** | **Cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities** (mostly **government securities**) |
| **Law (courseware)** | Central bank Act, s.42; Banking Regulation Act, s.18 | Banking Regulation Act, s.24 |
| **Held** | **Fortnightly average** (with a daily floor) | **At the close of business every day** |

The **statutory minimum and maximum limits were removed** (2006 and 2007), so the central bank can set the ratios **at its discretion**.

**Tools of monetary policy (quantitative):** **raising** CRR or SLR **impounds** cash and **absorbs liquidity**; **cutting** them **releases** funds and **infuses** liquidity. In extreme distress the central bank is **lender of last resort**. Current ratios change; **the courseware figures are not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: CRR is idle cash at the central bank; SLR is a stock of safe liquid assets that earn interest.

self_check.prompt_text: Which reserve is held as cash with the central bank and which in securities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: CRR is held as cash balances with the central bank; SLR is held in liquid assets such as government securities.

payload.title: Liquidity, inflation and the treasury duty on reserves
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity** is surplus funds with banks, a sign of money supply **not absorbed by the real economy**.

- **Excess liquidity** can cause **inflation**.
- **Shortage** can push **interest rates up** and **depreciate the rupee**.

The central bank adjusts **interest rates and policy stance** to the projected **growth** of the economy. With exchange controls largely removed it no longer targets a **specific exchange rate** but **monitors and smooths volatility**.

**Treasury duty:** meet the **CRR and SLR in full**; the **back office** submits the **fortnightly return** on time. A **default or shortfall** brings **penalties**, **damages reputation** and threatens **viability**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve compliance is a hard constraint, not an optimisation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the primary responsibility of treasury regarding reserve assets?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To meet the CRR and SLR requirements in full and submit the returns on time.

payload.title: Net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Demand liabilities** are payable **on demand**: **current deposits**, the **demand portion of savings deposits**, **margins against LCs and guarantees**, **overdue deposits**, **outstanding TTs, MTs and DDs**, **unclaimed deposits**, **credit balances in cash credit accounts**, deposits held as security payable on demand.

**Time liabilities** are payable **otherwise than on demand**: **fixed deposits**, **cash certificates**, **cumulative and recurring deposits**, the **time portion of savings deposits**, **staff security deposits**, margins not payable on demand, **gold deposits**.

**Money at call and short notice** from **outside the banking system** is shown against **liability to others**.

**NDTL** = the bank demand and time liabilities, **net of the deductions the central bank permits** (the detailed rules are in its directions). Some liabilities are **exempt or excluded** from the CRR base (such as liabilities to the **banking system**, **offshore banking units** and **ACU dollar balances**, and **capital, reserves and refinance**); the lists change and are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The reserve base is deposits and similar claims of the public, not the bank own funds.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a fixed deposit a demand or time liability?

payload.title: Computing and maintaining CRR and SLR, and the penalty
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Base and lag:** CRR (and SLR) are computed on **NDTL as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight**: a **one-fortnight lag** so banks can collect branch data.

**CRR maintenance:** kept on **average over the fortnight**, subject to **daily balances not below a stated share** of the requirement; the flexibility is for **scheduled commercial banks** and **not for urban co-operative banks**. Scheduled commercial banks keep CRR **only as balances with the central bank** (branch cash is not eligible; for urban co-operative banks it is). **No interest** is paid on CRR balances, so **CRR raises the cost of deposits**.

**SLR assets:** **cash (excluding CRR balances)**, **gold** (valued at not above market price) and **approved securities**.

**Penalty:** a **CRR shortfall** attracts **penal interest above the Bank Rate** on the shortfall (rising if it continues); an **SLR shortfall** attracts penal interest under the Banking Regulation Act. **A change in reserve ratios changes money supply**: a small **CRR cut releases a very large sum** (the courseware estimate: Rs 80,000-85,000 crore for 0.5 per cent) into **credit or investment**. Rates are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The lag means required reserves for a fortnight are known from earlier deposit data.

self_check.prompt_text: On which date is NDTL taken for the reserve computation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The last Friday of the second preceding fortnight.

payload.title: Required CRR and SLR from NDTL
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Required CRR = NDTL x CRR ratio.**

**Required SLR assets = NDTL x SLR ratio.**

**Total reserve assets required = NDTL x (CRR + SLR).**

**Funds available for lending and other investment = NDTL - required CRR - required SLR** (ignoring capital and other sources).

If the CRR is **cut by x per cent**, cash released = **NDTL x x**.

Example: NDTL **Rs 2,00,000 crore**, CRR **4 per cent**, SLR **18 per cent**: CRR **Rs 8,000 crore**; SLR **Rs 36,000 crore**; **free funds Rs 1,56,000 crore**.

assumptions: Ratios apply to the same NDTL base
Ratios are those assumed in the question
common_errors: Applying the ratios to total assets
Adding CRR to the SLR already counted in cash

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Ratios in the examples are assumptions; actual ratios change.

self_check.prompt_text: How much cash is released by a 1 per cent cut in CRR on an NDTL of Rs 1,00,000 crore?

payload.title: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **LAF** is the central bank **principal operating tool** for **day-to-day liquidity**; CRR and SLR change the stance more **permanently**.

- **Repo:** the central bank **lends** to banks against **government securities** (buys with an agreement to sell back): **injects** liquidity.
- **Reverse repo:** the central bank **absorbs** surplus funds (sells with an agreement to buy back).
- Securities stay in the **SGL account**: **no physical transfer**.
- **Interest** = sale and repurchase price difference.
- **Daily auctions** for overnight funds, sometimes more than once a day because banks need liquidity for **RTGS payment obligations**.
- The central bank may **change the term** and **accept or reject bids**.

| Short-term liquidity | Durable liquidity |
| --- | --- |
| **14-day variable rate repo or reverse repo** (main), **variable rate term repo** (fine-tuning), **fixed rate reverse repo**, **MSF**, **FX swap auctions**, **SDF** | **Long-term variable rate repo and reverse repo** (beyond 14 days), **FX swaps**, **open market operations** |

Amounts, rates and timings are as at 2022 and **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Repo gives banks cash against securities; reverse repo takes surplus cash back.

self_check.prompt_text: Which operation absorbs surplus liquidity from banks?

payload.title: The policy rate corridor: SDF, repo and MSF
payload.core_explanation_md:
Monetary policy aims to **narrow the corridor** and align the **weighted average call rate (WACR)** with the **repo rate**.

| Part of the corridor | Facility |
| --- | --- |
| **Ceiling** | **MSF rate**: the **maximum rate** at which banks can borrow **overnight** when other funds are unavailable |
| **Middle** | **Repo rate** |
| **Floor** | **SDF rate**: the **minimum rate** on **excess funds** parked with the central bank |

By keeping **overnight rates inside the corridor**, the central bank **reduces rate volatility**. By **moving the corridor** it raises or lowers interest rates **without directly regulating** each rate. Repo acts as the **market-based benchmark** for policy.

The central bank issues **master directions** for **call, notice and term money** operations of banks and primary dealers within **limits set by their boards**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A narrow corridor makes the overnight rate predictable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rate is the floor and which the ceiling of the corridor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The SDF rate is the floor; the MSF rate is the ceiling.

payload.title: Payment and settlement systems
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Payments** move money between banks and customers; **settlement** is the payment or receipt for **securities or foreign exchange**.

| System | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Cheque clearing (traditional)** | **Net settlement**, **1 to 3 day delays**, counterparty risk, high paper cost |
| **RTGS** | **Gross, real-time**, transaction by transaction; for **inter-bank and large** remittances; banks need **funds with the central bank all day**; **intra-day liquidity** via automatic repo |
| **INFINET / SFMS** | **Secure messaging** backbone; SFMS is like **SWIFT** |
| **NDS / NDS-OM** | **Electronic dealing** in government securities and money market instruments; **anonymous order matching** on **price and time priority**; **straight-through processing** to **CCIL** |
| **CCIL** | **Central counterparty** for government securities, repo and TREPS; clears forex via **FX Clear** on a **net basis** |
| **Depositories (NSDL, CDSL)** | **Delivery versus payment**: securities and funds move together, so **settlement risk is eliminated** |
| **NEFT** | **Same-day electronic transfer** (net batches) |

The central bank has a **board for regulation and supervision of payment and settlement systems**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Gross settlement removes the risk that a counterparty fails before day-end netting.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between gross and net settlement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Gross settlement settles each transaction individually in real time; net settlement offsets obligations and settles the balance later.

payload.title: Gross versus net settlement exposure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Gross settlement** moves each payment in full: **funds needed = sum of payments sent**.

**Net settlement** offsets obligations: **net position = payments received - payments sent**. Only the **net** is settled, so **less liquidity** is needed but **credit risk builds up** until settlement.

Example: Bank A sends **Rs 100 crore** and **Rs 60 crore** and receives **Rs 90 crore**: **gross** funds needed **Rs 160 crore**; **net** payment **Rs 70 crore**.

assumptions: All payments are between the same group of banks
common_errors: Treating the net as the gross liquidity requirement

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Gross settlement trades higher liquidity need for lower credit risk.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The liquidity needed, since only the net balance is paid.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Interest = 100 crore x 0.09 / 365 = Rs 2.47 lakh. The rates are assumptions for this exercise.
